title: Writing Process Vocabulary
keyIdea: Writers work in steps, and each step has a name. Plan means think of ideas and put them in order, the sequence. Draft means write it down, even if it is messy. Revise means make the words and ideas better, for example by adding detail. Edit, or proofread, means fix mistakes such as capitals, full stops and spelling. The audience is who will read it and the purpose is why you write it, which decides the kind: instructions tell how, a recount tells what really happened, and a story, or narrative, is made up.

kid: Writers do not write it all in one go. They do steps. First they plan. A plan is the ideas you think of. You put them in order: first, next, last. That order is the sequence.
Then they draft. A draft is your first go. You write it down. It can be messy. That is OK.
Next they revise. Revise means make it better. You can add a detail word, like big or fluffy. Then they edit. Edit means fix mistakes. Look for a capital letter, a full stop and the spelling.
Ask: who will read it? That is the audience. Ask: why am I writing? That is the purpose. Instructions tell how to do a thing. A recount tells what you did. A story is made up.
adult: This topic gives children aged 5 to 8 the words for the steps every writer takes: compose, plan, draft, revise, edit and proofread, plus audience, purpose, sequence, detail, paragraph and three kinds (genres) of writing: instructions, recount and narrative. Knowing the names helps children see writing as a process, not one sitting.

The lab is all taps with big targets. Children put plan, draft, revise and edit in order, plan a three-part kite story, add detail words to a draft and watch the picture change, tap three mistakes to edit a sentence, and match writing jobs to instructions, a recount or a story.

Common mistakes: mixing up revising and editing. Revising changes the ideas and words to make the writing better; editing fixes surface errors such as capitals, full stops and spelling. Many children also think the first draft must be neat, or that writing is finished once the last word is on the page. Some confuse a recount, which really happened, with a story, which is made up.

At home, when your child writes a card or list, use the words: shall we plan first? This is your draft. Can we revise it with one more detail? Now let's edit for capitals and full stops. Ask who the audience is before they start.

familyTip: Write a birthday card together in four steps: plan what to say, draft it on scrap paper, revise by adding one detail word, then edit for a capital letter and full stop before copying it neatly.

practice.hint: You think of ideas before you write.
practice.explain: First you plan: think of ideas and put them in order.

practice.prompt: Ava adds {n} detail words to make her writing better. What is she doing?
practice.hint: Making the words and ideas better has a special name.
practice.explain: Adding {n} detail words makes it better, so Ava is revising.

practice.prompt: Tom finds {n} spelling slips and fixes them. What is he doing?
practice.explain: Fixing {n} spelling slips is editing, also called proofreading.

practice.prompt: "First, get a cup. Next, pour the milk." What kind of writing is this?
practice.hint: Does it tell you how to do something?
practice.explain: It tells you how to do it in steps, so it is instructions.

practice.prompt: Kim writes a thank-you card to Gran. Who is the audience?
practice.hint: The audience is who will read it.
practice.explain: Gran will read the card, so Gran is the audience.

choices: Your first go at writing it down
pool.hint: It comes after the plan, and it can be messy.
pool.explain: A draft is the first go. It can be messy, and you make it better later.

pool.prompt: Leo's story has {n} sentences with no full stops. What should he do?
pool.hint: Full stops are mistakes you fix.
pool.explain: Adding the {n} missing full stops is editing.

pool.hint: Revising makes the words and ideas better.
pool.explain: Adding a detail word makes it better, so that is revising. The others are editing.

pool.prompt: What is the purpose of writing?
pool.explain: The purpose is why you write it. The audience is who reads it.

pool.prompt: "On Saturday I went to the park with Mum." What kind of writing is this?
pool.hint: Did it really happen to the writer?
pool.explain: It tells what really happened, so it is a recount.

pool.prompt: Sam's plan has {n} ideas. He puts them in order: first, next, last. What is that order called?
pool.hint: It is the order things happen in.
pool.explain: Putting the {n} ideas in order makes a sequence.

pool.prompt: "Once upon a time, a cat could fly." What kind of writing is this?
pool.hint: Ask yourself: can a cat really fly?
pool.explain: It is made up, so it is a story, also called a narrative.

pool.prompt: Mia wrote her draft. Is her writing finished?
choices: No, she can revise and edit it
pool.hint: Writing has more steps after the draft.
pool.explain: After the draft she revises to make it better and edits to fix mistakes.

visual.caption: Revise or edit? Ask: does it make it better, or fix a mistake?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: put the writing steps in order, plan a story, revise with detail words, edit three mistakes and match each job to its kind of writing.
